title: Sorting While Preserving the Original Data

blocks.text: std::sort sorts the elements in the specified range. For a numeric vector, we write std::sort(datos.begin(), datos.end()); and include <algorithm>. The default order is ascending: no later element is smaller than its predecessor. The operation modifies the vector; it does not automatically create a sorted copy.

begin() and end() provide library positions delimiting the range: from the beginning (included) to the end (excluded). They differ from the indices we display as numbers. end() is past the last element; it is not a value to read. We do not yet need to manipulate these positions ourselves to use this complete call.
The output is 2;5;7;. The collection still has three values; only their order changed.

blocks.explanation: Sorting keeps both occurrences of four and preserves the number of elements.

blocks.question: What does sort do with duplicate values?
options: It keeps them, placing them in sorted order.
It converts them into indices.
It automatically deletes all but one.
blocks.explanation: Sorting and removing duplicates are different tasks.

blocks.question: Fill in only the name of the sorting operation used in the previous example.
blocks.explanation: sort orders the entire range specified by begin and end.

blocks.question: Predict the exact output, without adding quotation marks.
blocks.explanation: An empty range can be sorted and remains empty; no element is accessed.

blocks.question: You sort {1, 2, 2, 8}, which is already in ascending order. What can you expect?
options: It keeps the same values and remains sorted.
It must become {8, 2, 2, 1}.
It must lose the duplicates.
blocks.explanation: Sorting again need not visibly change a collection that is already sorted.

blocks.text: The original order may carry information

If the data represent sessions in arrival order, sorting the vector changes which value belongs to the first session. To preserve that information, make a copy and sort the copy. std::vector<int> ordenados = original; preserves the values at that moment in another object.

blocks.question: Predict the exact output, without adding quotation marks.
blocks.explanation: auto deduces a separate collection by value; sorting it does not modify original.

blocks.question: The report must preserve measurement order and also show sorted values. Which choice meets both needs?
options: Sort the original and assume it still represents arrival order.
Rename original to cronologico after sorting it.
Sort a copy and keep the original.
blocks.explanation: Renaming an object does not restore the information you changed.

blocks.text: Strings can also be sorted. The default comparison is lexicographical: it compares characters, and when strings share a prefix, the shorter string comes first. These examples use lowercase Latin letters without accents. We do not claim this comparison follows language-specific collation rules for accented or uppercase text.

blocks.question: Predict the exact output, without adding quotation marks.
blocks.explanation: Both occurrences of cat come before cats, which shares their prefix but is longer; cats sorts before dog.

blocks.question: You sort the text labels "10" and "2". Which rule does string comparison use?
options: The length of the variable's name.
Always the magnitude of the numbers they appear to represent.
Their characters, without automatically converting them to quantities.
blocks.explanation: The chosen representation determines the operations: numeric-looking text remains text.

blocks.text: Display distinct values without deleting data

After sorting, equal values are adjacent. To display each value only once, print the first and then only those that differ from their predecessor. In i == 0 || datos[i] != datos[i - 1], short-circuit evaluation of || avoids examining i - 1 when i is zero. This display does not remove elements from the vector.

blocks.question: Predict the exact output, without adding quotation marks.
blocks.explanation: Three distinct values are displayed; the vector still contains five elements.

blocks.question: What protects the access datos[i - 1] when displaying the first value?
options: The first true condition stops the evaluation of ||.
sort makes every subscript valid.
The vector creates a position -1.
blocks.explanation: This protection depends on the order of evaluation and short-circuit behavior.

blocks.text: Counting distinct values is a separate question

blocks.question: Predict the exact output, without adding quotation marks.
blocks.explanation: There are four observations but only two distinct values.

blocks.question: With an empty vector, how many distinct values does this traversal produce?
options: Zero, because there are no visits.
One because of the condition i == 0.
An invented value of zero.
blocks.explanation: The body condition is never evaluated if the loop visits no elements.

blocks.text: Build a program preserving two orders

Make a sorted copy of {6, 2, 6, 1}. Display Original:6;2;6;1; and Sorted:1;2;6;6; on separate lines. Add a third line, Distinct:3. Repeat with {}, {4}, and {5, 5}: these contain zero, one, and two observations, respectively, but have zero, one, and one distinct values.
For further practice, use the labels {"b2", "a1", "b2"} with <string>. Explain what information the original preserves and why displaying distinct values does not change its size.

blocks.question: When reporting an index after sorting, what must you say about it?
options: It describes the collection in its current order.
It is always the value that was found.
It must be the original arrival position.
blocks.explanation: An index describes a position in a particular sequence.

blocks.text: Lab criteria: sort a copy by value, preserve the original sequence and all repeated observations, count distinct values without deleting them, and protect access to the previous neighbor; the same rules must hold for text labels.
